Launched in the United States in 1996 (Science World, Oct 1996: “introduced around the country last May”); announced for Canada on April 14, 1997, on sale May 1, 1997

None: Orbitz was a product, not a company. Its maker filed a creditor proposal in March 2010, had its shares cancelled on May 26, 2010 and was acquired by Robert R. Khan in 2012 (per Fast Company).
No current owner found. The maker’s 2006 application for ORBITZ was abandoned on Dec 8, 2008; Fast Company reported in 2024 that the old owners sold the trademark (buyer not named).

timelineAdd.text: Bush Boake Allen Inc. files a US patent application, “Method of suspending inclusions,” on keeping particles afloat in beverages. A student newspaper later says a patented Bush Boake Allen recipe made the Orbitz gel spheres.
Science World says Orbitz was introduced around the United States “last May.”
A University of Arizona summer paper covers Orbitz as one of the summer's new test-market drinks.
Science World leaves a bottle standing: the spheres sink part way and stop.
The oldest Wayback capture of orbitz.com, the drink’s “Welcome Page,” is saved.
Clearly Canadian announces the Canadian launch, with sales from May 1 at 7-Eleven, Shoppers Drug Mart and Famous Players cinemas.
A Washington-area distributor says it has carried Orbitz for six weeks and it is “moving very well.”
Course participants at the University of Minnesota ask how 5 mm gel balls stay suspended in Orbitz; the answer is published in January 1999.
The Planet Orbitz site offers an “Orbiterium” tour, in one version for Netscape and one for Internet Explorer.
A lawsuit with Bush Boake Allen, which Clearly Canadian says had charged it with patent infringement in making Orbitz, is settled with a licensing fee, according to a company-history reference.
Clearly Canadian buys back distribution rights in several Mid-Atlantic states, completing control of its North American distribution.
A rheology newsletter prints the measured yield stress of the Orbitz liquid: 0.04 Pa.
A company-history reference says Orbitz sales were suspended because of dwindling sales, with a significant writedown.
orbitz.com is a domain-service placeholder: “registered by a member of myinternet.com.”
The airline-backed travel venture is officially named Orbitz, LLC and Orbitz, Inc.
orbitz.com shows “Soon the difference will be clear ©2000 Orbitz, LLC.”
Clearly Canadian’s shares are delisted from Nasdaq and move to the OTC Bulletin Board.
Brent Lokash becomes president, replacing Douglas Mason as chief executive; the company later describes Orbitz as a drink that “seemed to defy gravity.”
Clearly Canadian files a US trademark application for ORBITZ covering soft drinks and non-carbonated fruit beverages.
Clearly Canadian buys DMR Food Corporation, an organic snack maker; BevNET reports total revenue rose for the first time in a decade while beverage revenues fell.
The USPTO issues a notice of allowance for ORBITZ; a statement of use is due.
The ORBITZ application is abandoned because no statement of use was filed.
Clearly Canadian files a creditor proposal under Canada’s Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act; creditors approve on April 1, the court on April 26, and existing shares are cancelled on May 26.
Robert R. Khan acquires the Clearly Canadian company (per Fast Company).
An unrelated individual files ORBITZ DEFY GRAVITY DRINK ORBITZ for beverages on March 5 and abandons it on May 9.
The SEC revokes the registration of Clearly Canadian Beverage Corp.’s securities (Jan 4); the brand resumes full-scale production the same year.
Fast Company reports the Orbitz trademark was sold and the machine that made the spheres was sold for parts.

now.title: The drink
now.text: Not made. In 2015 a company representative said it lacked the equipment; in October 2024 Clearly Canadian’s marketing chief said the machine that made the spheres broke down and was sold off for parts.

now.title: The name
now.text: The maker’s 2006 application for ORBITZ was abandoned on Dec 8, 2008, and an unrelated 2014 application was withdrawn within two months. Fast Company says the old owners sold the trademark; the buyer is not named and we could not find a live ORBITZ beverage registration.

now.title: The maker, 2010 to 2017
now.text: Clearly Canadian Beverage Corporation filed a creditor proposal on Mar 17, 2010, its shares were cancelled on May 26, 2010, and the SEC revoked its registration on Jan 4, 2017.

now.title: The Clearly Canadian brand
now.text: Acquired in 2012 by Robert R. Khan, back in full production in 2017 and, as of October 2024, owned by a group of private investors. Clearly Canadian said it was on track to sell about 45 million bottles in 2024.

now.title: orbitz.com
now.text: The drink’s Planet Orbitz site was at orbitz.com from December 1996; by February 2000 the address was a parked page and by January 2001 it carried the airline-backed Orbitz, LLC. No source we could open says how the address changed hands.

now.title: The bottles
now.text: An unopened 1990s bottle sells for around $50 on eBay, according to Gastro Obscura (undated).

now.title: The people
now.text: Douglas Mason, who founded Clearly Canadian and led it as chief executive, was replaced in that role in October 2005 when Brent Lokash became president. Jonathan Cronin, the marketing executive quoted on Orbitz, moved to the US subsidiary in December 1998.

glossary.def: A liquid that carries a weak, invisible gel structure. It pours like a liquid but stops suspended particles from sinking.
A gel-forming hydrocolloid that the Associated Press named as the material of the Orbitz spheres.
The smallest force a gel-like liquid needs before it starts to flow. Below it, particles held in the liquid stay where they are.
The study of how materials flow and deform.
Pieces of solid matter, such as fruit bits or gel spheres, suspended in a drink.
The industry label for premium non-cola drinks such as flavored sparkling water, iced tea and functional drinks.
The annual report that a company based outside the United States files with the SEC when its shares trade in the US.
A report in which such a company furnishes news, such as press releases, to the SEC.
A Canadian procedure in which a company offers its creditors a deal to settle its debts, without being wound up.
A reverse split: old shares are exchanged for fewer new ones, which raises the quoted price without changing what an owner holds.
An electronic quotation service for shares that are not listed on a major exchange.
The filing that proves a trademark is in commercial use. An applicant who filed before using the mark must send it after the notice of allowance or the application is abandoned.

edges.caveat: The supply and the lawsuit rest on a company-history reference (secondary) and a student paper; the patent record shows only that Bush Boake Allen owns a suspension patent.

insights.summary: Orbitz puzzled rheologists, and they measured why it worked. A University of Minnesota paper found the liquid has a yield stress of 0.04 Pa, about twice what keeps “builder” particles suspended in liquid detergent, yet at a shear rate of 100 per second it is only four times as viscous as water, so it pours like water. For 5 mm balls the liquid can carry a density mismatch of about 12 kg/m3. The question came from two course participants in August 1997; the paper was printed in January 1999. A 1996 Science World test showed the spheres do sink part way, then stop.
insights.where: Story chapter 1 'In the lab'; numbers section view 'The physics' (counters); glossary terms fluid gel, yield stress

insights.summary: The drink’s website became the travel company’s address. Planet Orbitz lived at orbitz.com from at least December 1996 to January 1999; by February 29, 2000 it was a domain-service placeholder; by January 2001 it read “©2000 Orbitz, LLC.” The travel venture was named Orbitz in July 2000. The sources we could open do not say how the address changed hands, and the Wayback Machine has no capture between Feb 9, 1999 and Feb 29, 2000.
insights.where: Website section / signature recreation; where-are-they-now card 'orbitz.com'; story chapter 5

insights.summary: The name was kept alive on paper and never used again. The company's 20-Fs for 2005, 2006 and 2007 still listed Orbitz among its innovations; it applied to register ORBITZ on Sept 29, 2006, won a notice of allowance on May 6, 2008, and let the application lapse on Dec 8, 2008 by not filing a statement of use. In 2024 the brand's current marketing chief said the trademark was sold and the machine was sold for parts.
insights.where: Where-are-they-now cards 'The name' and 'The drink'; story chapter 6; what-if 'Keep the machines'

insights.summary: While Orbitz faded, so did its maker, and a competitor named in its own 20-F did the opposite. From 1998 to 2002 Clearly Canadian's revenue fell 41% (34.889 to 20.477, $M), while Hansen Natural's net sales rose 89% (48.628 to 92.046) and the US new age beverage market grew from $3.8 billion in 1992 to an estimated $13.1 billion in 2002. Revenue rose in 2007 after two food acquisitions; BevNET reported beverage revenues down 25 percent (the article does not say over what period).
